authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro — unreviewed candidate generation

items.prompt: An outer loop advances right from 0 to n−1. Inside it, a while loop advances left, but left never moves backward and advances at most n times total. What is the total time complexity of the boundary movement?
constraints: Each right increment and each left increment performs O(1) maintained-state work.
No helper scans the current window.

feedback.reason: The nested while loop is amortized over monotone pointer movement: right advances n times and left advances at most n times.

blocks.text: Syntactic nesting does not multiply iteration counts when the inner pointer keeps its progress. `right` contributes n moves and `left` at most n, so O(1) work per move gives O(n+n)=O(n). O(1) and O(log n) cannot cover the n right increments; O(n^2) incorrectly multiplies two loop bounds even though `left` never resets. The bound would change if `left` restarted for each right or a helper rescanned the current window.

items.prompt: A longest at-most-K-distinct window uses a hash map of frequencies. Assume expected O(1) hash operations and no more than K+1 keys during a transient violation. Select its expected time and extra-space complexities.
constraints: The map stores only keys currently represented in the window and removes zero-count keys.

feedback.reason: Monotone boundary movement gives expected O(n) time, while the active frequency map contains O(K) distinct keys.

blocks.text: Each element enters once and leaves at most once, so at most a constant multiple of n expected-O(1) map operations gives expected O(n) time. O(n log n) would match logarithmic ordered-map updates, not the stated hash assumption; O(n^2) would require resets or repeated interior scans. After repair there are at most K keys and a transient violation has at most K+1; because K≥1, K+1≤2K and space is O(K). O(1) applies only when K or the alphabet is fixed independently of input, while O(n) is a looser bound that ignores the declared K cap. In concrete domains the state is also bounded by the alphabet size.

items.prompt: There are n−k+1 fixed-length windows. An implementation recomputes each window sum by visiting all k elements instead of using a rolling update. What is the tightest offered time bound in terms of both n and k?
constraints: No prefix sums or rolling state are used.

feedback.reason: The implementation performs k visits for each of exactly n−k+1 candidate starts, so its tight two-parameter bound is O((n−k+1)k).

blocks.text: The exact work is proportional to `(n-k+1)k`: there are `n-k+1` starts and each rescan visits k values. `O(nk)` is a valid loose upper bound but not the tightest over the full domain: when k=n, only one window exists and the exact expression is O(n), whereas nk is O(n²). O(n) is not sufficient for all k because the expression reaches Θ(n²) near k≈n/2; O(k) ignores multiple starts, and O(n²k) adds an unsupported extra factor. Rolling add/remove state or prefix sums reduce each post-initialization window query to O(1), making the complete scan O(n).

items.prompt: A frequency window is described as O(n) because each map update is O(1). Which statement is the precise complexity qualification?
constraints: The implementation uses a general-purpose hash map.
The analysis distinguishes expected from adversarial worst-case behaviour.

options.text: Hash lookup is worst-case O(1), so the algorithm is unconditionally worst-case O(n).
The traversal is expected O(n) under expected O(1) hash operations; a pathological hash-map worst case can be worse unless the map contract provides stronger bounds.
Using any map automatically makes each operation O(log n), so the algorithm is O(n log n).
The shrink loop makes the algorithm O(n²) regardless of map cost.

feedback.reason: The pointer count is linear, but the total bound inherits the operation guarantee of the chosen frequency structure.

blocks.text: The algorithm performs O(n) state operations because each element enters and leaves at most once. With an ordinary hash map, those operations are commonly analyzed as expected O(1), yielding expected O(n) time. A balanced ordered map would instead give O(n log K), while a fixed-array alphabet can provide deterministic O(1) updates. Claiming unconditional worst-case linear time requires a data-structure contract that supports it. The nested loop alone does not cause quadratic work.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.worst_case_always_linear: General hash tables do not universally promise worst-case constant-time operations under all collision patterns.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.map_makes_nlogn: Ordered maps often cost logarithmic time, but hash maps are normally expected constant time; the structure must be named precisely.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.nested_means_n2: Left does not restart, so its total moves remain O(n); only the per-operation state cost changes the bound.

items.prompt: Both boundaries move only forward, but after each right step the code scans every element currently in the window to recompute whether it is valid. What can happen to the time complexity?
constraints: Window length can be Θ(n) for Θ(n) different right positions.
The full-window scan is separate from pointer movement.

options.text: It remains O(n) solely because left and right are monotone.
A validity predicate over a window is automatically O(log n).
It can be O(n²) because Θ(n) right steps may each perform a Θ(n) validity scan.
If left rarely moves, the repeated scans become O(1).

feedback.reason: Monotone boundaries bound pointer moves, not hidden work that repeatedly traverses the interior of the current range.

blocks.text: The usual O(n) proof assumes O(1) or otherwise bounded state maintenance per element entering or leaving. If each outer iteration rescans a window that can contain Θ(n) elements, the sum of scan lengths can be Θ(n²), even when left never moves backward. Rare shrinking can make this worse by keeping windows large. To recover linear or near-linear time, maintain the validity-driving statistic incrementally or use a structure with a stated update/query cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_linear: Pointer monotonicity accounts only for boundary operations; it does not amortize independent full-window scans.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_logarithmic: Predicate cost depends on the data structure and implementation; no logarithmic guarantee is automatic.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant_if_no_shrink: A stationary left boundary leaves a growing window, so rescanning it can cost more, not less.
